extracted.intended_audience: general readers, industry observers, and researchers interested in HBO Max/Max streaming service operations and history
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of HBO Max/Max service distribution, product features, accessibility commitments, pricing/tiers, release-window and licensing policies, and international rollout decisions. The page documents operational policies and contractual arrangements governing availability and content delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility commitments (audio description hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of a settlement with the American Council of the Blind, at least 1,500 hours of HBO Max content would be available with audio description (AD) by the end of March 2021, increasing to at least 6,000 hours by March 2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement also required other accessibility enhancements to website and apps by September 2021; HBO Max later began rolling out AD on select titles starting March 26, 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for signed and other accessible content (ASL, BASL)
rubrics_metrics.description: HBO Max offers selected content with American Sign Language (ASL) interpretation; season 2 of The Last of Us became the first television series on a streaming service to offer a signed version of its first-run episodes. In June 2025, Sinners was announced as the first film to be offered on a streaming platform in Black American Sign Language (BASL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents an accessibility feature set beyond closed captioning and AD, with examples and timeline for rollout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for advanced audio/video formats
rubrics_metrics.description: At launch, HBO Max did not support 4K, HDR, Dolby Vision, or Dolby Atmos, but support for these technologies was planned as part of the HBO Max product roadmap. Support for 4K, HDR, and Atmos was added starting with Wonder Woman 1984.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates technology compatibility expectations and staged content format availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same-day premieres / 'Project Popcorn' policy
rubrics_metrics.description: In late 2020 WarnerMedia moved some Warner Bros. films to exclusive or simultaneous releases on HBO Max (a decision referred to internally as 'Project Popcorn'), releasing titles either exclusively or simultaneously with theaters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The move prompted backlash from filmmakers and industry groups; Warner Bros. spent significant compensation for talent; subsequently the studio discontinued same-day releases in 2022 as part of agreements with exhibitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical release-window policy (45-day/exclusive-window and case-by-case decisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Warner Bros. announced a 45-day exclusive release window for theaters in 2022 (after Project Popcorn), but only used it for two films; following restructuring, the length of the window would be decided for each film on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that release-window policy is subject to change and negotiation per film and corporate strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ad-supported tier feature limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The ad-supported tier would include HBO original programming remaining ad-free for subscribers of that tier, but the tier would not allow access to Same-Day Premieres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines functional limitations of lower-priced/ad-supported plans relative to premium features like same-day releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing structure for ad-supported and ad-free tiers
rubrics_metrics.description: WarnerMedia announced the ad-supported tier would launch at $9.99 a month, with yearly options priced at $99.99 (ad-supported) and $149.99 (ad-free).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides concrete price points and the existence of yearly subscription options at launch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution-agreement contingency for customer access
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to HBO Max for many existing HBO pay TV subscribers is contingent on the customer's current provider or biller having signed a new distribution agreement for HBO Max with WarnerMedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why entitlement/migration to HBO Max at no extra charge depended on carriage/distribution deals with pay-TV and other providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform/device support and compatibility requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: HBO Max availability depends on device/platform compatibility (e.g., available on fourth-generation Apple TV and fifth/sixth generation Apple TV 4K; earlier Apple TV versions that do not support third-party app download are not supported).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Device generation and platform capability constrain which customers can access the app natively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform carriage negotiation points (commissions and ad-revenue sharing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes with platforms (e.g., Roku) over making HBO Max available were reported to hinge on carriage commissions and advertising sales on the future ad-supported tier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights negotiation levers (commissions, ad inventory/sales) that determine platform carriage and timing of availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: International rollout strategy: direct launches vs licensing to third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: In many countries Max/HBO programming was either launched as a localized HBO Max/Max service or licensed to third-party networks and streaming services under long-term deals; Warner Bros. Discovery at times halted direct expansion in favor of licensing to reach financial stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that availability varies by market depending on existing HBO agreements, local partners (Sky, Foxtel, Bell/Crave), and strategic decisions to license rather than direct-launch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional promotional pricing (Europe 50% 'for life' offer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The European launches featured a promotion offering the service with a 50% discount 'for life' for new subscribers as long as they maintain their subscription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of market-specific promotional tactics to drive adoption during rollout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-sharing and pay-one window agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Disney and WarnerMedia amended pre-existing contracts to allow Disney+ or Hulu and HBO Max to share streaming rights to half of 20th Century Studios' and Searchlight Pictures' 2022 theatrical slate in the United States during the pay-one window (e.g., Ron's Gone Wrong was made available on both Disney+ and HBO Max).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates how studio licensing and cross-service deals affect where theatrical films appear during pay-one windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports content packaging and tiering strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans were announced to launch a sports-focused tier (Bleacher Report Sports add-on) with live events and studio shows; following portfolio changes the paid add-on launch was delayed and later scrapped, with live sports made available at no additional charge as part of Standard and Premium tiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates evolving strategies around bundling premium live sports—plans may change based on rights portfolio and corporate strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional branding and trademark constraints affecting rollout
rubrics_metrics.description: The Max rebranding was retained as 'HBO Max' in the Netherlands due to trademark conflicts with Omroep MAX and VRT MAX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that local trademark and branding conflicts can alter naming and rollout decisions in specific markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content distribution via third-party channels and bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: In some markets Max/HBO content was distributed through third-party services or subscription channels (e.g., Le Pass Warner on Amazon Prime Video in France, Crave in Canada), with arrangements sometimes converting to native Max availability upon launch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how existing local distribution arrangements affect where and how content is available and how transitions occur when Max launches natively.
